title: Review your goals like a friend
description: A regular, kind review turns goals from a source of pressure into a conversation you actually look forward to.

body.heading: Reviews are steering, not judging
paragraphs: Many people avoid reviewing their goals because the review feels like a verdict: on track means good, behind means lazy. With that framing, of course we postpone it. The review becomes the thing we are failing at, on top of everything else.
Try a different job description. A review is steering. A sailor checks the compass often, not to feel bad about the wind, but to adjust the sails while adjusting is still cheap.

body.heading: A fifteen-minute monthly conversation
paragraphs: Once a month, take your goals somewhere pleasant — a walk, a café, the garden — with three questions. What moved, even a little? What got in the way, honestly? What is the kindest useful next step for each goal?

Write the answers down, briefly. Writing matters because memory edits the past to match our mood; notes from last month tell the truth, including about progress that felt invisible while it was happening.

body.heading: Let goals change their shape
paragraphs: A good review sometimes ends with a goal getting smaller, slower or even retired — and that is the review working, not failing. Goals were set by a past version of you with less information than you have now.

End by choosing one next step per goal, small enough to start this week. Then close the notebook. The goals are held safely in the system now, and your mind is free to just live until next month’s conversation.

takeaway: Review monthly, with curiosity instead of a scorecard — and let the goals adjust.
